newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Tietmeyer says sees solution with Bonn on assets.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer says sees solution with Bonn on assets.

text.p: Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said he had the impression the bank could find a solution with the Bonn government to controversial plans to raise cash by revaluing the central bank's assets.

Tietmeyer, speaking at a banking meeting in Interlaken, Switzerland, said he had indications that German Finance Minister Theo Waigel would not force a transfer of profit in 1997, as had originally been planned.
It was not clear whether a change in the Bundesbank law would be required, he added.
"I have the impression that we can find a solution. Whether it needs some change of Bundesbank laws must be investigated," he said.
"We have had some indications from Waigel that he is not interested in introducing legislation that would force us to do that (transfer profit) in 1997," he added.

Tietmeyer said it would not be appropriate to meet targets laid down for European monetary union by simply creating money, citing one of the objections originally raised by the central bank to Bonn's call for a transfer of revaluation profits in 1997, the key year for qualification for monetary union.
"To meet the criteria via creating money is not the best solution. Thus we have made clear that it would not be appropriate to deliver more profit this year."
He rejected the idea that the central bank should draw up a special mid-year balance sheet to enable a transfer, saying this would not be appropriate if it was aimed at meeting the EMU goals.
"We are willing to do so (revalue) but we say it is not appropriate to do that mid-year and to do that for a special purpose to finance the present budget," he said.

"We have always said that revaluation of some assets seems to be appropriate as the risks have changed and will change," Tietmeyer added. "Of course this would then mean there is potential for a higher profit in the next years."

Reiterating that no final agreement had yet been made with Bonn on a plan which would allow a revaluation at the end of 1997 and a profit transfer in 1998, Tietmeyer said he nonetheless hoped that the EMU schedule could be met with appropriate application of the criteria for entry.
He also made clear that Bonn and the Bundesbank were absolutely in agreement on the idea that there should be no sales of gold.
Asked in general about the revaluation plans, he said, "This is not just a question of gold, this is a question of other assets too."
Bonn has been forced to retreat from its original plans to get extra funds from a revaluation of Bundesbank assets this year. Full details of the new plan are not yet clear.
